concepts.decision: Control entry, changes, cabling, environment, maintenance, and alert response.
concepts.definition: Protection of cabling, network equipment, and intermediate distribution facilities.
concepts.failureExample: An unlocked closet lets an intruder connect a rogue network device.
concepts.label: Wiring Closet Security

concepts.decision: Combine entry controls, environment, power, zoning, operations separation, and response.
concepts.definition: Layered protection of data-center facilities, equipment, operations, utilities, and maintenance.
concepts.failureExample: A data center has strong doors but uncontrolled vendor maintenance access.
concepts.label: Data Center Security

concepts.decision: Use custody and protection based on classification, recovery risk, and lifecycle.
concepts.definition: Controlled storage of removable media or data-bearing assets through inventory, access, retention, and disposal.
concepts.failureExample: Backup tapes sit in an unlocked office before offsite transfer.
concepts.label: Media Storage

concepts.decision: Use when records may support investigation, legal, or disciplinary reliance.
concepts.definition: Preservation of evidence with integrity, access control, retention, and chain of custody.
concepts.failureExample: An incident log is copied among analysts with no custody record.
concepts.label: Evidence Storage

concepts.decision: Apply zoning, visitor rules, clean desk/display practices, and logical protection by sensitivity.
concepts.definition: Controls for normal work spaces, screens, documents, visitors, and local devices.
concepts.failureExample: A visitor photographs visible records from an unattended workstation.
concepts.label: Work Area Security

concepts.decision: Provide maintenance, monitoring, alarms, redundancy or response suited to thermal consequence.
concepts.definition: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning capability affecting equipment environment and people.
concepts.failureExample: Cooling loss overheats equipment while no monitored alert reaches operators.
concepts.label: Hvac

concepts.decision: Select compatible detection, response, suppression, personnel safety, and asset effects.
concepts.definition: Detection and suppression or containment measures for fire risk.
concepts.failureExample: Suppression is installed but no tested alert/response process exists.
concepts.label: Fire Suppression

concepts.decision: Plan utility, UPS, generator, fuel, transfer, load priority, testing, and recovery.
concepts.definition: Ability to sustain or safely recover power-dependent services through redundancy, backup, and maintenance.
concepts.failureExample: A generator has no fuel assurance or tested transfer under load.
concepts.label: Power Resilience

concepts.decision: Connect monitored thresholds to accountable response and test the full signal path.
concepts.definition: Sensing and alerting for temperature, humidity, water, smoke, power, or other conditions.
concepts.failureExample: A water sensor alarms locally but nobody receives or acts on it.
concepts.label: Environmental Monitoring

concepts.decision: Choose identity assurance, zones, escort, logging, review, emergency behavior, and anti-tailgating measures.
concepts.definition: Authorization, authentication, and recording of physical entry to protected areas.
concepts.failureExample: A shared badge gives untraceable access to a server room.
concepts.label: Physical Access Control

concepts.decision: Test normal, emergency, maintenance, alert, and recovery behavior with evidence.
concepts.definition: Testing whether a facility control is designed, operating, and responsive as intended.
concepts.failureExample: A control passes installation but fails when a responder is unavailable.
concepts.label: Control Assessment

misconceptions.correction: Availability also depends on capacity, transfer, fuel, maintenance, testing, upstream utilities, and recovery priorities.

outcome: Select a coordinated control set for a facility asset and explain the response or recovery dependency that makes it effective.

sections.body: Wiring closets and server rooms need controlled access, environmental protection, documented maintenance, and alert response. Media and evidence storage need inventory, custody, protection against disclosure or alteration, retention, and authorized disposal. Restricted work areas combine visitor control, clean-desk or display practices, escorting, and logical protections. The right combination depends on asset sensitivity and consequence of loss, change, or delay.
keyPoints: Evidence storage requires integrity and custody as well as confidentiality.
A secure room still needs authorized maintenance and documented access.
sections.title: Protect specialized spaces and assets

sections.body: Utilities, HVAC, water, fire, smoke, temperature, humidity, power, and natural or human-caused events affect availability and safety. Use prevention, detection, suppression or containment, redundant or backup capability, maintenance, monitoring, and tested response. A generator without fuel, tested transfer, maintenance, and load priorities is not a resilient power strategy.
keyPoints: Environmental controls have operational and life-safety dependencies.
Detection is useful only when a response owner and procedure exist.
sections.title: Plan environmental resilience and response

sections.body: Wiring closets and intermediate distribution facilities need controlled entry, protected cabling and equipment, and monitored changes. Server rooms and data centers need layered entry, environmental and power resilience, operations separation, and secure maintenance. Media and evidence storage require inventory, access control, integrity, retention, and chain-of-custody appropriate to consequence. Restricted and work areas require zoning, visitor controls, clear-desk or screen practices where applicable, and response paths. Utilities and HVAC need resilience, maintenance controls, and safe failure behavior; natural and human environmental threats drive location, structural, monitoring, and recovery choices. Fire prevention, detection, and suppression must protect people and equipment with appropriate response procedures. Redundant and backup power must be sized, tested, maintained, and tied to shutdown or recovery priorities. A deployed device is not a control until its owner, test, alarm response, and maintenance evidence exist.
keyPoints: State the protected property, boundary, decision owner, operating evidence, and residual failure mode.
Treat architecture controls as lifecycle commitments: configuration, monitoring, response, maintenance, and recovery determine whether the claim holds.

teaching.focalRelation: Prevention and environmental capacity reduce exposure; detection must notify an accountable responder; containment/suppression depends on people and life safety; power and HVAC resilience depend on transfer, fuel, maintenance, testing, and upstream utilities; recovery verifies readiness.

learningJob.plainExplanation: A sensor or redundant component is useful only when it triggers accountable response and works through the full dependency chain. Generator nameplate capacity does not prove transfer, starting load, runtime, fuel, alarms, or maintenance.
